newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN tries peacemaker role in Cambodia crisis.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN tries peacemaker role in Cambodia crisis.

text.p: Despite its oft-stated aversion to intervening in the affairs of its neighbours, the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) is prepared to do just that in Cambodia's latest crisis.
After an emergency meeting in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday, ASEAN foreign ministers said they still recognised the ousted Norodom Ranariddh as co-premier in Cambodia.

They also decided to send the foreign ministers of Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand to meet with Cambodian head of state King Norodom Sihanouk, who is in Beijing receiving medical treatment, and then with the two feuding prime ministers.
That is bound to aggravate Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who warned ASEAN before the meeting that Cambodia's problems were its "internal business".
"ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."
At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded when Hun Sen's troops took control of Phnom Penh in battles last weekend. Ranariddh left for France on the eve of the fighting.

Hun Sen accused Ranariddh of provoking his own overthrow, echoing a foreign ministry white paper obtained earlier on Thursday that said Ranariddh has destabilised Cambodia by building up his own army and conducting secret talks with the reviled Khmer Rouge.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said ASEAN was making an exception to its rule of non-interference in a neighbour's internal affairs because force was used.

"Our policy of non-interference remains...but there's a dramatic change in the political situation in Cambodia and that has been brought about by the use of military force," he told reporters after the meeting.

One Western diplomat, however, noted that ASEAN has declined to use that criterion in the case of Burma, whose military rulers have been accused of widespread human rights abuses in their brutal crackdown of a pro-democracy movement led by Nobel Laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
The ASEAN foreign ministers decided to penalise Cambodia for its descent into political chaos by postponing the country's admission into the seven-member group.
But Burma and Laos will be admitted as scheduled at ASEAN's annual series of meetings July 21-29 in Kuala Lumpur.
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

ASEAN has maintained that members cannot interfere in each other's domestic affairs, especially when governments of current members range from a communist one-party state in Vietnam, an absolute monarchy in Brunei, an authoritarian government in Indonesia and democracies in Thailand and the Philippines.
But the group has a long history of diplomatic involvement in Cambodia.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was an architect of the accords that Washington said on Tuesday had been ruptured by Hun Sen.
In the 1980s, ASEAN supported a guerrilla coalition led by King Sihanouk that included Ranariddh's faction and the Khmer Rouge against the Vietnamese-backed government in Phnom Penh led by Hun Sen.
But whether a sick and politically marginalised Sihanouk can again put the humpty dumpty of Cambodian politics back together again -- with or without ASEAN's help -- is questionable, diplomats said.
"Effectively, the monarchy is finished," said one diplomat in Phnom Penh. "I cannot see Sihanouk returning to give legitimacy to this government," he said.

The king still retains widespread respect amongst his people, especially in the countryside, and some analysts suggested Hun Sen would like nothing more than to see the king out of the political picture once and for all.
Hun Sen announced Ranariddh's ouster in a Sunday television broadcast and bluntly rejected Sihanouk's offer to hold reconciliation talks with the two premiers.
